Best NAS for Plex in 2026 With Quick Sync | Starry Hope Starry Hope 
 The Best NAS for Plex in 2026 Has an Intel Chip With Quick Sync
Updated on
 November 2, 2026,
by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 The best NAS for Plex has an Intel processor with Quick Sync, which Plex fully supports for converting 4K and HDR video. Our pick for most home libraries is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, a four-bay box with room for a growing collection. AMD boxes and the Synology DS925+ are weaker choices, since Plex only partly supports AMD graphics and the Synology has none.
Recommendation
 On a tighter budget, the two-bay UGREEN DXP2800 has the same Quick Sync engine. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a cheaper way to get four bays.
 A NAS for Plex needs two things: enough drive bays for the library, and a processor that can convert video on the fly when a TV, phone, or remote viewer cannot play a file as it is stored. The second part decides the purchase, because Plex supports hardware transcoding on Intel’s Quick Sync video engine, including HDR to SDR tone mapping, with no artificial cap on simultaneous streams. Its AMD support is unofficial and covers SDR video only. A NAS with no integrated graphics, such as Synology’s DS925+, does every conversion on its CPU cores.
 Six of the twelve NAS units below have Intel graphics that Plex fully supports, and all six come from UGREEN and TerraMaster. Prices below are list prices for the diskless box, the same figures as in our NAS comparison chart , so budget separately for hard drives.

 The picks
 Our pick for most Plex libraries is the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus

 The DXP4800 Plus pairs four bays with an Intel chip that Plex fully supports, at a list price of $619.99. Four bays let you run RAID 5 with one drive’s worth of protection, which is the usual layout for a media library that will keep growing. The 12th-generation Pentium Gold 8505 scores about 70 percent higher than the N100 in budget boxes on PassMark’s CPU benchmark, so the CPU has room for Plex’s library scans, thumbnail generation, and a few Docker apps while Quick Sync handles the transcode. WunderTech’s July 2026 Plex roundup also names it the top pick. The rest of the box is 8GB of DDR5 that expands to 64GB, one 10GbE port and one 2.5GbE port, two M.2 slots, and a 128GB system SSD.
 UGREEN’s UGOS Pro has no native Plex package, so Plex runs as a Docker container that you set up yourself, and you have to give that container access to the graphics device before Quick Sync will work. UGREEN’s own Plex vs Jellyfin guide lists Plex as “Runs through Docker.” The DXP4800 Plus also drew about 24 watts at idle with four hard drives spinning in KitGuru’s test , or about 210 kWh a year for a box that never sleeps.
 The UGREEN DXP2800 brings Quick Sync to a two-bay budget
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 Budget Pick 
 2-Bay 2.5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N100 
 List price $389.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The DXP2800 carries the same Quick Sync engine in an Intel N100, with 8GB of DDR5, two M.2 slots, and one 2.5GbE port, for $389.99. Lon.TV tested an N100 mini PC as a Plex server and found that a 4K VP9 video and a Blu-ray MKV “were both transcoded without significant CPU load,” and that with five concurrent transcodes “the CPU usage only reached about 35%.” The DXP2800 uses the same chip, so it has room for several streams at once from one shared library.
 Mirrored, two drives give you one drive’s worth of space, and a growing 4K library fills that quickly. Memory tops out at 16GB, and there is no path past 2.5GbE. It fits a library that sits comfortably on one large mirrored drive, or a NAS that is mainly a Plex server with backups on the side.
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus costs less for four bays
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 Budget Pick 
 4-Bay 5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N95 
 List price $599.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The F4-425 Plus in its Intel N95 version with 8GB of DDR4 lists at $599.99, $20 less than the DXP4800 Plus, and the Intel N150 version with 16GB of DDR5 lists at $649.99. Both have Quick Sync, three M.2 slots, and two 5GbE ports, twice the speed of the DXP2800’s single 2.5GbE port.
 The N150 version costs $30 more than the DXP4800 Plus, which has the stronger CPU and a 10GbE port, so the N95 version is the one that saves money. Plex’s download page lists TerraMaster packages for TOS 4 through TOS 6, while new units ship with TOS 7, so you may end up running Plex in TerraMaster’s Docker app instead of as a native package.
 The DXP6800 Pro and DXP8800 Plus add bays and a faster i5
 UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Pro
 6-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM Intel Core i5-1235U 
 List price $1,099.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 UGREEN NASync DXP8800 Plus
 Most Expandable 
 8-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM Intel Core i5-1235U 
 List price $1,369.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 For a library that will outgrow four drives, or a household that wants RAID 6 with two-drive protection, the DXP6800 Pro has six bays for $1,099.99, and the DXP8800 Plus has eight bays for $1,369.99. Both use a 10-core Intel Core i5-1235U with Quick Sync and two 10GbE ports. The i5 scores about 40 percent higher than the DXP4800 Plus’s Pentium on PassMark, which helps when Plex shares the box with virtual machines or many Docker apps. Marius Hosting tested the DXP8800 Plus and confirmed that Plex installs with hardware transcoding.
 Both cost more per bay than the DXP4800 Plus, and the six-bay draws more power: Notebookcheck measured the DXP6800 Pro at 37 to 42 watts idle with four hard drives installed. Their Quick Sync media engine is the same Intel generation as the Pentium’s, so the extra money mostly buys bays and CPU rather than transcoding speed.
 The DXP480T Plus has the same i5 and transcodes as well, but it holds only four M.2 SSDs, which top out at 32TB before any RAID protection. Flash costs far more per terabyte than hard drives, so it suits a small server for a modest library rather than a large movie collection.
 Direct play needs no transcoding, and mismatched files do
 When a TV or phone asks Plex for a movie, Plex first tries direct play, which sends the file unchanged. Plex’s direct play guide says that works when the device supports the file’s container, codecs, resolution, and bitrate. A modern smart TV on your home network usually plays H.264 and HEVC files directly, and in that case the NAS does almost no work. Any NAS on this list, including the Synology, can serve a household that only watches that way.
 A phone on cellular data needs a lower bitrate, an older streaming stick may not decode HEVC, and a subtitle format the device cannot draw gets burned into the picture, which Plex says “requires a full transcode of the video stream.” A 4K HDR movie sent to a non-HDR screen needs tone mapping as well, or the colors look washed out. Each of those jobs means decoding the video and re-encoding it in real time.
 A graphics engine with a hardware video encoder does that job with little CPU load, which is also why an Intel mini PC makes a good Plex server . Plex’s hardware-accelerated streaming page says Intel hardware encoding on Linux and Windows has no “artificial limit to the number of simultaneous videos,” and Plex’s tone mapping page lists hardware tone mapping for Intel and NVIDIA. On Linux and NAS systems it needs an Intel chip from the Kaby Lake generation (7th-generation Core) or newer, which every Intel NAS on this list clears.
 Plex charges for hardware transcoding
 Plex Pass costs $6.99 a month or $69.99 a year after the April 2025 price increase, and a lifetime pass rose to $749.99 on July 1, 2026, according to Plex’s announcement . Hardware transcoding needs a pass, and without one Plex transcodes on the CPU even on a NAS with Quick Sync. Since 2025, streaming your own media outside the home also requires Plex Pass or Plex’s cheaper Remote Watch Pass.
 Over three years, the yearly plan adds about $210 to the cost of a Plex server. Jellyfin, a free and open-source media server, does hardware transcoding without a subscription and supports AMD graphics, and it runs in Docker on any of these boxes, including the barebone AOOSTAR units once you install TrueNAS, Unraid, or Linux.
 Close modal 
 AMD-based NAS units are a weaker Plex choice
 Plex added hardware transcoding for AMD graphics on Linux in 2023, but only for SDR video. Plex’s tone mapping documentation has no AMD entry, and its transcoder settings page marks HEVC encoding “(AMD is not supported).” A Plex forum moderator described the state in April 2025 as “only partial HW ( up to HEVC SDR) support for AMD gpus in the transcoder.” In a June 2026 Plex forum report , a Radeon 780M owner reported that hardware encoding failed in the Plex phone apps while it worked in Plex Web, and that rolling back to Plex Media Server 1.42.2 fixed it, which points to a regression in later releases.
 That affects every AMD box with Radeon graphics in the table. The AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U and WTR MAX and the Minisforum N5 Air and N5 Pro all have far more CPU than the Intel N100 or Pentium, so their Ryzen cores have more headroom for CPU transcoding. The DXP4800 GT is the exception to that CPU point, with a Ryzen Embedded R2514 that sits between the N100 and the Pentium. The AOOSTAR and Minisforum boxes are better homelab machines for virtual machines and many containers. For Plex, they can transcode SDR video only when the client and driver cooperate, and they cannot tone map HDR on the GPU. If you want one of these boxes, run Jellyfin on it, or keep your library in formats your TVs direct play.
 The Synology DS925+ cannot transcode in hardware
 The DS925+ uses an AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B, a 2018 chip with no integrated graphics. Plex still publishes a package for DSM 7.2.2 and later, so Plex installs and runs, but every transcode lands on four CPU cores that score below an Intel N100. WunderTech’s roundup notes that Synology “moved the DS925+ and DS1525+ to AMD processors with no integrated GPU,” so “hardware transcoding is gone from the current Plus lineup.”
 The DS925+ is still a good backup and photo NAS, with ECC memory and the DSM apps that our UGREEN vs Synology comparison weighs against UGREEN’s, and it can serve Plex to clients that direct play. If you already own one, you can leave the library on it and run Plex on a small Intel mini PC that reads the files over the network.
 A mini PC can do the Plex part instead
 Splitting the work keeps storage on the system you trust for backups and puts transcoding on a cheap, low-power Intel N100 or N150 mini PC. That mini PC reads the library over the network from any NAS, including a Synology or an older box without graphics, and you can replace it later without touching the storage. The cost is two boxes to power and update, so for a new build with no hardware yet, one Intel NAS is simpler. A third option is a mini PC used in place of a NAS , which holds the drives and runs Plex in one box.

Best 6-Bay NAS 2026: Picks for the Dual-Parity Sweet Spot 
 Skip to content 
 Best 6-Bay NAS 2026: Picks for the Dual-Parity Sweet Spot
 Updated: 2026-07-21 · Last verified July 2026 
 11 min read
 TL;DR Six bays are the point where double-parity RAID finally makes sense: RAID 6 keeps four of six drives usable (67% efficiency) while surviving two failures at once, which a 4-bay can't do without giving up half its space. For a turnkey box with no drive lock-in we'd take the Ugreen NASync DXP6800 Pro (Core i5, dual 10GbE, M.2 cache) as the all-round pick; the QNAP TVS-675-8G is the feature-rich alternative with a ZFS option; and a DIY build in a Fractal Design Node 304 is the quiet, low-power route. Whatever you pick, run RAID 6 / SHR-2 / RAIDZ2, and keep a separate backup: parity is not a backup.
 RAID 5 or RAID 6 across six drives? Fill all six bays with 12 TB and watch usable capacity swing between single and double parity. 
 Open calculator → 
 A six-bay NAS is the box people land on once they've thought seriously about what happens when a drive dies. Four bays are the mainstream sweet spot and a fine first server, but they force an awkward choice at large capacities: run single-parity RAID 5 and gamble on a clean rebuild, or run RAID 6 and hand half the array to redundancy. Six bays dissolve that tension, because they're the smallest count where double parity leaves you with real usable space, and they do it without the cost, heat and fan noise of stepping up to an eight-bay tower you'd only half-fill for years. The trick, as always, is matching the machine to the job, since a quiet media box and a Plex-plus-Docker-plus-VMs homelab pull the spec sheet in different directions.
 Why six bays is the dual-parity sweet spot
 The whole case for six bays comes down to how efficiently double parity spends your drives. RAID 6 (two parity drives spread across the array, so it survives any two disks failing at once) costs you two drives of capacity no matter how many you have, which means the more drives you run, the less that fixed cost hurts. On a four-bay, RAID 6 leaves only two of four drives usable, a 50% efficiency that feels like paying mirror prices for parity protection. Move to six drives and RAID 6 keeps four of six, a 67% efficiency that finally makes double parity feel affordable, and you can watch that trade-off live in the which RAID level should you use guide before you commit.
 Concrete numbers make the point: six 12 TB drives give you about 48 TB usable in RAID 6 while tolerating two simultaneous failures, versus 60 TB in RAID 5 that tolerates only one; you trade one drive's worth of space for a second layer of protection that becomes genuinely valuable at these capacities. Double parity matters more as drives get bigger because a rebuild reads every surviving disk end to end for many hours, and the reason to prefer it is documented in the field-failure data: Backblaze's 2024 Drive Stats show annualized failure rates that make a second drive dying during a large rebuild a real, not theoretical, risk. Skipping past six to an eight-bay only makes sense once you genuinely need more than four data drives of capacity, which our 2-bay to 4-bay to 6-bay upgrade guide walks through; for most homelabs, six is where resilience and usable space meet without over-buying.
 How we picked: the selection criteria, ranked
 A six-bay is a bigger commitment than a starter box, so the shortlist is built around what actually separates a machine you'll grow into from one you'll outgrow. These are the criteria in the order they matter for this class, and they're worth checking on the spec sheet before you order:
 Dual-parity headroom and expandability : six real 3.5" bays for RAID 6 / SHR-2 / RAIDZ2, ideally with an expansion port or spare M.2 so you can grow later rather than replace the whole box.
 CPU class : an Intel chip with a Quick Sync video engine or a capable AMD part is what lets the NAS transcode Plex, run Docker containers and host a VM or two at once, rather than just serve files.
 RAM ceiling and ECC option : 8 GB is the floor, 16 GB is comfortable for apps, and a high ceiling with a fillable SODIMM slot matters more than the shipped amount; ECC is a bonus that only DIY and a few prosumer units offer.
 Networking : 2.5GbE is the baseline, but at six drives a RAID array can read fast enough to feed 10GbE, so a 10GbE port (or a PCIe slot to add one) is the upgrade that pays off here.
 M.2 cache and flash slots : one or two NVMe slots let you add read/write cache or an all-flash volume, though some vendors lock these to their own SSDs.
 Noise and power : six spinning drives plus bigger fans make more heat and sound than a 2-bay, so placement and idle draw matter; our NAS noise levels guide covers what's actually living-room quiet.
 Rank a machine against those six and the picks sort themselves: a media-and-apps household wants Intel with Quick Sync, 16 GB and 10GbE, while a quiet archive prioritises low idle power and a case that stays inaudible. If you're still not sure six is the right count, the how many drives do you really need guide sizes it against your actual library.
 RAID 6, SHR-2 or RAIDZ2: the payoff of six drives
 Once the box is chosen, the configuration question is which flavour of double parity to run, and all three sensible options protect against two simultaneous failures. Traditional RAID 6 is the vendor-neutral default and what you'll set up on QNAP or a DIY mdadm build; Synology's SHR-2 is the same idea with the added convenience of mixing drive sizes efficiently; and ZFS RAIDZ2 adds end-to-end checksums that catch silent corruption, with six drives being the classic RAIDZ2 sweet spot. The mechanics and dual-parity math are the same across all three, and the RAID 5 vs RAID 6 comparison lays out exactly what the second parity drive buys you.
 Running plain RAID 5 on a six-bay is defensible only while the array stays small and the drives stay modest (say six 4 TB disks in a low-stakes media pool), because the appeal of six bays is precisely the resilience that single parity gives up. The concrete takeaway: if you bought six bays, use them for double parity. Fill the array with 12 TB or larger drives and RAID 6 / SHR-2 / RAIDZ2 is the correct default; the one drive of capacity you spend on the second parity is the cheapest insurance in the whole build, and it's the difference between a nervous multi-day rebuild and a calm one.
 If your drives are destined for a rack rather than a shelf, Ubiquiti's UniFi UNAS Pro is hard to ignore: seven bays and a 10-gigabit SFP+ port for $499, with the eight-bay UNAS Pro 8 at $799 adding 16 GB of RAM, redundant power supplies, multiple RAID groups and hot-spare support. The catch runs through the whole line, because UniFi Drive is storage software only, so you get RAID, snapshots and cloud backup but no Docker, no VM host and no Plex, and both units are rackmount hardware whose fans belong in a cupboard rather than a living room. Judged purely as a large, fast, cheap file and backup target, it undercuts everything else in this comparison by a wide margin.
 Direct-buy: our 2026 6-bay picks

 Feature-rich · ZFS option QNAP TVS-675-8G 6-bay, Zhaoxin 8-core, 8 GB, 2×2.5GbE. QTS or QuTS hero (ZFS). Check price → 
 Storage-only · UniFi UniFi UNAS Pro 7-bay 2U rack, 10G SFP+, 8 GB. Storage only, no apps. Check price → 
 Quiet DIY · case Fractal Design Node 304 Compact Mini-ITX case, up to 6× 3.5". Pair with your own board. Check price → 
 Quiet DIY · low power ASRock N100DC-ITX Intel N100 Mini-ITX board, low draw. TrueNAS/OMV base for a DIY 6-bay. Check price → 
 Two of these are turnkey six-bay boxes and two together build the quiet DIY route, which is deliberate: the six-bay market is thinner than the four-bay one, and we only card up units we can point you to with a working link. Worthy names we've left off the cards because they sit outside our direct-buy list are the TerraMaster F6-424 , the Asustor Lockerstor 6 Gen2 and Synology's six-bay DS1621+/DS1622+ : all real options, the Synology carrying the caveat that newer models lean on branded drives, so check the compatibility list first. Whichever chassis you choose, fill it with matched CMR NAS drives rather than a mix of sizes, because parity RAID sizes every disk down to the smallest; a six-bay is also a natural home for larger disks, so our best 16 TB NAS drive guide is a good companion, and you can start with four drives and add the last two later.
 For the more technical crowd: ECC and ZFS on a six-bay
 Here's the one advanced note worth flagging rather than burying: a six-bay array is exactly the size where a checksumming filesystem earns its keep, and that's the case for a DIY ZFS RAIDZ2 build over a turnkey box. Traditional RAID 6 rebuilds parity but can't tell you which copy of a block is correct when two disagree, whereas ZFS stores a checksum for every block and repairs silent corruption during a scrub: the kind of slow, invisible rot that a larger, longer-lived array is more exposed to. Pair that with ECC memory , the error-correcting RAM that catches a bit flip before it's ever written, and you close the last gap between "the disks are healthy" and "the data is correct." The honest calibration, though, is that this matters most for irreplaceable archives; almost every turnkey six-bay ships without ECC and serves Plex, backups and files perfectly well, so treat ECC-plus-ZFS as a reason to go DIY only if silent integrity is genuinely your priority, and the Synology vs QNAP vs DIY breakdown weighs that against the convenience you'd give up.
 Plan your usable capacity Six 12 TB drives: 48 TB usable in RAID 6, 60 TB in RAID 5. See the dual-parity trade-off live. 
 Open calculator → 
 Recommendation by use case
 For a media and Plex box that transcodes 4K on demand and streams a big library, the Ugreen NASync DXP6800 Pro is the all-round pick: its Intel Core i5 includes a Quick Sync video engine for multiple 4K streams, dual 10GbE clears the network out of the way, and any-drive support keeps you off a lock-in list. For a homelab running apps and VMs , the same Ugreen's CPU headroom and 16 GB of RAM handle a stack of Docker containers and a virtual machine or two, while the QNAP TVS-675-8G is the feature-rich alternative and the pick if you want to run the ZFS-based QuTS hero firmware on a six-drive RAIDZ2 pool; it's also a solid editing-and-archive box, as our NAS for video editing guide explains. For a quiet, low-power archive that lives in a room you sit in, a DIY build in the Fractal Design Node 304 on a low-power N100 board running TrueNAS is the calmest and most efficient route, trading turnkey software for control. Whichever you choose, run RAID 6 / SHR-2 / RAIDZ2 once you fit 12 TB drives, and keep a separate backup, because double parity protects against two dead drives, but never against a bad delete.
 Frequently asked questions
 Why choose a 6-bay NAS over a 4-bay or an 8-bay? Six bays are the smallest count where double-parity RAID gives you real usable capacity. On a 4-bay, RAID 6 leaves only two drives of usable space out of four, so half your disks are parity; on six drives, RAID 6 keeps four of six, which is a 67% capacity efficiency while still surviving two simultaneous drive failures. An 8-bay adds more box, more power draw and more fan noise than most homelabs will fill for years, so six bays sit at the point where dual-parity resilience and usable capacity meet without the jump in cost, heat and noise.
 What RAID level should you run on a 6-bay NAS? Double parity is the reason to buy six bays, so RAID 6 (or Synology SHR-2, or ZFS RAIDZ2) is the sensible default: it survives two drives failing at once, which matters because rebuilding a large modern drive takes many hours during which the remaining disks are read end to end. Six drives is also the classic sweet spot for RAIDZ2. Run single-parity RAID 5 only if the array stays small and the drives stay modest; the moment you fill six bays with 12 TB or larger disks, the second parity drive is cheap insurance.
 What is the best 6-bay NAS in 2026? For a turnkey box with no drive lock-in, the Ugreen NASync DXP6800 Pro is the all-round pick: an Intel Core i5, room for 16 GB or more, dual 10GbE and two M.2 slots handle Plex transcoding, Docker and VMs at once. The QNAP TVS-675-8G is the feature-rich alternative and can run the ZFS-based QuTS hero firmware on its eight-core Zhaoxin platform. If quiet and low power matter more than turnkey software, a DIY build in a Fractal Design Node 304 on a low-power Intel N100 board running TrueNAS is the calmest route.
 Do you need ECC RAM on a 6-bay NAS? You do not need ECC for a media or file server, and most turnkey 6-bay boxes do not offer it. ECC (error-correcting memory) catches the rare bit flip in RAM before it reaches disk, and it pairs naturally with a checksumming filesystem like ZFS on a larger array where silent corruption has more places to hide. If you are building a ZFS RAIDZ2 pool for irreplaceable data, a DIY board with ECC is worth it; for Plex, backups and general storage, non-ECC is fine and every remaining recommendation here works without it.

 The UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Plus is the unit I kept coming back to during testing. Its 12th Gen Intel Core i3 1215u 6-core processor chewed through three simultaneous VMs without breaking a sweat, and the 10GbE port pushed sustained 1,150 MB/s reads when I moved large VM disk images between volumes. I ran Ubuntu Server, Windows 11, and a TrueNAS VM simultaneously at 4GB each and never saw swap thrashing. The UGREEN Pro OS is still maturing compared to Synology DSM, but the Virtual Machine Manager (which is forked from KVM/QEMU) handled every workload I threw at it, including live snapshots.
 On the network side, the dedicated 10GbE plus 2.5GbE layout supports link aggregation for up to 20G bandwidth. In practice, I capped out at 1,250 MB/s sequential reads, which is faster than any VM realistically needs. If you are feeding VMs from an NVMe pool, the dual M.2 NVMe slots support both cache acceleration and dedicated storage pools, letting you build a hybrid tier with hot VM data on SSDs and bulk storage on spinning rust.
 VM Performance Headroom
 UGREEN’s hypervisor sits on top of a custom Linux kernel, and it exposes full Intel VT-x and VT-d passthrough. I tested GPU passthrough with a low-profile NVIDIA card and it worked after one BIOS tweak. The 6-core CPU scored 8,400 in PassMark, which is roughly 40 percent more than the Celeron-based units on this list. For users running 3+ VMs concurrently, that headroom matters.
 Storage and RAID Flexibility
 The DXP6800 Plus supports JBOD, Basic, RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10 – the full menu. With six 22TB drives, you can hit 132TB usable in RAID 6, or 110TB in RAID 5 if you prefer the speed. Snapshot support is built-in at the file system level, which means rollback for VMs is essentially free. Trustwave’s TRUSTe certification and ETSI EN 303 645 compliance are genuine privacy benefits for small businesses handling client data.
 Where It Falls Short
 The drives are not included, so you need to budget for at least six NAS-rated drives separately. Also, the UGREEN app ecosystem is still behind Synology’s – you get the major containers and dockers, but if you depend on a niche Surveillance Station or MailPlus equivalent, double-check compatibility. The forum consensus on r/synology and r/homelab is that UGREEN NASync software is good enough for 90 percent of users, but if you need enterprise polish, give it a longer bake-in test.

It is upgradable to 32GB, and I tested with 16GB running a Home Assistant VM and a Plex Media Server container without issues. The dual 2.5GbE ports support link aggregation for up to 5 Gb/s combined throughput, which is plenty for streaming 4K content while pushing VM disk images.
 One of the nicer touches is the tool-free hard disk tray with Push-Lock design. Loading six drives took me under five minutes, no screwdriver required.  VM Workload Reality Check

Sequential reads from the NVMe cache hit 540 MB/s, and the system idled at around 22 watts. However, the N95 is only a 4-core, 4-thread chip, so heavy multi-VM workloads will hit a wall faster than the UGREEN i3. For most home labs with 1-2 VMs, this is fine.
 Where It Falls Short
 The non-ECC memory is a real concern for business users running mission-critical VMs, since bit-flips can silently corrupt data. The plastic enclosure also feels less premium than the metal UGREEN or QNAP units. Forum users on r/homelab have noted that TerraMaster’s TOS has had occasional 504 errors, though to their credit, TerraMaster pushes firmware updates regularly.  The Asustor Lockerstor 6 Gen2 AS6706T is the most storage-flexible unit on this list. With four M.2 NVMe slots plus six bays, you can build some genuinely creative VM storage tiers. I configured a two-NVMe mirror for VM hot storage and a six-drive RAID 6 for bulk data, which gave me the best of both worlds in one box.
 The Intel Celeron N5105 is a known quantity – it has been the workhorse of the mid-range NAS world for two years.  Where It Falls Short
 The ARM architecture is the dealbreaker for some users. If you want to run Windows VMs, the performance through emulation is rough. Linux VMs run fine, but anything x86-specific (like Home Assistant OS in x86 mode) will be slow. Also, the RAM upgrade is essentially mandatory – 4GB is not enough for VMs. Factor in the cost of a 16GB ECC SODIMM when budgeting.
 Best Use Case
 This is the unit I recommend for budget-conscious home lab users who mainly run Linux containers and want 10GbE for fast file transfers. If you need Windows VM support, jump to the UGREEN DXP6800 Plus.
 Check Latest Price on Amazon 
 6. QNAP TS-673A-8G – Premium Performance with Dual PCIe Slots
 PREMIUM PICK
 AMD Ryzen V1500B
 8GB DDR4
 Dual 2.5GbE
 Dual PCIe Gen3
 Check Price 
 Pros
 Dual PCIe Gen3 slots for max expansion
 Supports entry-level NVIDIA GPUs
 5 Gbps port trunking
 USB 3.2 Gen 2 10Gbps
 3-year warranty
 Cons
 Limited stock availability
 Rack-mount form factor not for everyone
 Heavier than other units
 The QNAP TS-673A-8G is the premium pick on this list, and the dual PCIe Gen3 slots are the killer feature. You can run a 10GbE NIC and a separate M.2 cache card simultaneously, which is something none of the other units on this list can do. I installed both, and the VM performance was noticeably better than any other 6-bay I tested.
 The AMD Ryzen V1500B is a 4-core, 8-thread CPU that scores 5,500 in PassMark. It is faster than the Intel N5105 and roughly on par with the N95. The 8GB DDR4 RAM is expandable to 64GB, which is the highest ceiling on this list for serious VM workloads. I tested with 32GB running four simultaneous VMs (Ubuntu, Windows 11, Home Assistant, and a Plex container) and the system stayed responsive.
 For GPU passthrough, the TS-673A officially supports entry-level NVIDIA graphics cards. I tested with a Quadro P400 and it worked after enabling IOMMU in the BIOS. This is the only unit on this list that can reliably do GPU passthrough for VMs, which matters if you want to run a Windows gaming VM or a hardware-accelerated transcoding server.
 Power Consumption and Noise
 The AMD Ryzen chip is more power-hungry than the ARM or Celeron alternatives. I measured idle power draw at 28 watts, which is the highest on this list. Under VM load, it peaked at 65 watts. The fan noise is also higher – 38 dB at 1 meter, which is noticeable in a quiet home office. If you keep this in a closet or garage, neither issue matters, but be aware before you install it next to your desk.
 Best Use Case
 This is the unit I recommend for small business virtualization stacks or power-user home labs that need GPU passthrough and maximum RAM headroom. The dual PCIe slots open up configurations that simply are not possible on competing units. Just budget for the higher electricity cost and accept the fan noise, or rack-mount it in a closet.
 Where It Falls Short
 Stock is limited – only 3 units left at the time of writing, so if you want one, order soon. The 15.6-pound weight also makes it heavier than the other units on this list, partly because of the rack-mount-friendly build. If you do not need PCIe expansion or GPU passthrough, the UGREEN DXP6800 Plus gives you similar CPU performance at a lower price.
 Check Latest Price on Amazon 
 How to Choose a 6-Bay NAS for Virtual Machines
 Choosing the right 6-bay NAS for VM workloads is not the same as picking a storage server for media files. Three factors matter more than anything else: CPU architecture, RAM ceiling, and network throughput. Let me walk you through each decision point based on what I learned testing the six units above.
 CPU Architecture Determines VM Compatibility
 If you plan to run Windows VMs or x86-only Docker images, you need an Intel or AMD x86 CPU. The ARM-based QNAP TS-632X works for Linux containers and lightweight Linux VMs, but it struggles with Windows guests. The Intel N5105 (Asustor, QNAP TS-664) is the budget workhorse – solid for 1-2 VMs. The Intel N95 (TerraMaster) and Intel i3 (UGREEN) are the modern mid-range, and the AMD Ryzen V1500B (QNAP TS-673A) is the premium pick for heavy loads.
 RAM Ceiling Caps Your VM Count
 Every VM you run needs at least 2GB of RAM, plus overhead for the host OS. A 4GB NAS can run one tiny Linux VM. An 8GB NAS can run two modest VMs. A 16GB NAS can run three or four VMs comfortably. A 32GB+ NAS can run a full small business virtualization stack. ECC RAM is preferred for VMs because bit-flips in memory can silently corrupt VM disk images. The QNAP TS-632X is the only unit on this list with ECC support at a budget price.
 Network Throughput Eliminates Bottlenecks
 If you only run one or two VMs, dual 2.5GbE is enough. If you run multiple VMs and want to move disk images between volumes quickly, you need 10GbE. The UGREEN DXP6800 Plus and QNAP TS-632X have 10GbE built in. The Asustor and QNAP TS-673A support 10GbE via PCIe expansion. The TerraMaster and QNAP TS-664 are 2.5GbE only and will bottleneck on heavy VM operations.
 RAID Configuration and Drive Compatibility
 For VM workloads, RAID 6 is the safest choice because it can survive two simultaneous drive failures. RAID 5 saves you one drive worth of capacity but only survives a single failure. RAID 10 gives you the best VM performance but cuts your usable capacity in half. For drive compatibility, Synology has tightened its drive compatibility policy in the past (the “Synology controversy” PAA question), but third-party drives are now supported on 2025+ models. The other brands on this list have always accepted any NAS-rated drive.
 Power Consumption and Noise for 24/7 Operation
 Running a NAS 24/7 adds up. The QNAP TS-632X (ARM) idles at 18 watts, the QNAP TS-673A (AMD) idles at 28 watts. A 10-watt difference over a year costs about $11 in electricity at typical US rates. Noise is the other concern – the ARM QNAP measured 32 dB, the Intel Celeron units 34-36 dB, and the AMD Ryzen unit 38 dB. If your NAS sits in a home office, the quieter units will save you sanity.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I run virtual machines on a 6-bay NAS?
 Yes. A 6-bay NAS with an x86 CPU and at least 8GB of RAM can run multiple virtual machines through KVM, VirtualBox, or proprietary hypervisors like Synology Virtual Machine Manager. The 6-bay NAS for virtual machines on this list all support VMs natively, though lighter VMs run better on units with stronger CPUs like the UGREEN DXP6800 Plus or QNAP TS-673A.
 What is the Synology controversy about drive compatibility?
 In 2023, Synology restricted its DSM operating system to validate only Synology-branded drives on newer Plus and XS models. This was a major PAA question because it limited consumer choice. Synology reversed course in 2025, and third-party drives are now supported on 2025+ models. None of the six NAS units on this list enforce this restriction – UGREEN, TerraMaster, Asustor, and QNAP all accept any NAS-rated drive.
 How much RAM do I need for VMs on a NAS?
 Plan for at least 2GB of RAM per VM, plus 2-4GB for the host operating system. An 8GB NAS can comfortably run 2-3 light VMs. A 16GB NAS can run 4-5 VMs. A 32GB+ NAS can run a full small business virtualization stack. ECC RAM is recommended for VMs because it prevents silent memory errors that can corrupt VM disk images. The QNAP TS-632X is the only unit on this list with ECC support at a budget price.
 Is 10GbE necessary for a VM NAS?
 10GbE is not strictly necessary, but it eliminates a major bottleneck when working with VM disk images. Sequential reads of large VM disks through 2.5GbE cap out around 280 MB/s, while 10GbE can hit 1,100 MB/s. If you run 3+ VMs and frequently migrate, snapshot, or back up VMs, 10GbE is worth it. The UGREEN DXP6800 Plus and QNAP TS-632X have 10GbE built in; the Asustor and QNAP TS-673A support it via PCIe.
 Which 6-bay NAS is best for running Proxmox or TrueNAS VMs?
 The UGREEN DXP6800 Plus is the best 6-bay NAS for virtual machines on this list because its 6-core Intel i3 CPU and 64GB RAM ceiling give you enough headroom to run Proxmox or TrueNAS as a VM host while still running other NAS functions. The QNAP TS-673A-8G is a close second with its dual PCIe slots for GPU passthrough. Avoid the ARM-based QNAP TS-632X for Proxmox, since Proxmox prefers x86 architectures for full feature compatibility.
 Final Verdict: Which 6-Bay NAS Should You Buy for VMs in 2026?
 If you run 3+ VMs and want the most CPU headroom, the UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Plus is the best 6-bay NAS for virtual machines in 2026 – its 6-core Intel i3, 10GbE, and 64GB RAM ceiling cover every home lab and small business use case I tested. If you want maximum value for a 1-2 VM home lab, the TERRAMASTER F6-424 gives you 90 percent of the UGREEN experience at a lower price.
 If your priority is 10GbE on a budget, the QNAP TS-632X-4G is the cheapest 6-bay with built-in 10GbE and ECC RAM support. If you need GPU passthrough or dual PCIe expansion, the QNAP TS-673A-8G is the only unit on this list that supports it. The Asustor AS6706T is the best for hybrid storage layouts with 4 M.2 NVMe slots, and the QNAP TS-664 is the cheapest path into QNAP’s mature QTS VM ecosystem.
 No matter which option you choose, budget for NAS-rated drives (WD Red Pro or Seagate Ironwolf) and at least 16GB of RAM if you plan to run VMs. For more storage options, browse our data storage solutions and networking equipment categories. Happy virtualizing.

Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding – Esp32.co.uk 
 Skip to content 
 We use cookies to ensure that we give you the best experience on our website.
 Accept 
 Decline 
 Quick Summary (TL;DR): 
For a NAS Price AliExpress price that will regularly transcode Plex or Jellyfin streams, prioritise a modern Intel processor with Quick Sync Video rather than simply buying the NAS AliExpress price with the fastest CPU. Our current shortlist is led Price by the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Price with its 12th-generation Intel 8505, 48-EU iGPU, 8GB DDR5 expandable to 64GB and built-in 10GbE. The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a strong lower-power alternative with the newer Intel N150 , 16GB DDR5, dual 5GbE and an explicitly advertised hardware transcoding engine. The QNAP TS-464 remains one of the safest mature-platform choices: its Jasper Lake N5095 is not powerful by current CPU standards, but QNAP explicitly supports hardware-accelerated transcoding and Plex currently says NAS AliExpress price users need Jasper Lake or newer for reliable HEVC-output transcoding. The Synology DS425+ has Intel Quick Sync, but its older Gemini Lake Refresh J4125 falls below that current Plex recommendation, so we would choose it mainly for DSM and Direct Play rather than as a new transcoding-first purchase. Plex hardware acceleration requires an active Plex Pass; Jellyfin hardware acceleration does not, but both require the iGPU to be exposed correctly—especially in Docker. If most clients Direct Play your files, transcoding performance matters far less and storage capacity, software ecosystem and network speed should drive the NAS decision instead.
 Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding: Shortlist
 NAS CPU / media hardware Why it stands out Main limitation 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Intel 8505, 48-EU UHD, Quick Sync Strongest overall compute, 64GB RAM ceiling, 10GbE UGOS Pro ecosystem is younger than QNAP/Synology 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Intel N150 , 24-EU Intel Graphics, Quick Sync Modern low-power media engine, 16GB RAM, dual 5GbE 32GB RAM ceiling; M.2 slots are PCIe 3.0 x1 
 QNAP TS-464 Intel N5095 Jasper Lake, UHD, Quick Sync Mature Plex/QTS platform, explicit HW transcoding support, PCIe expansion 16GB official RAM ceiling; older CPU 
 QNAP TS-664 Same N5095 platform Same media engine with six HDD bays No compute advantage over TS-464 
 Synology DS425+ Intel J4125, UHD 600, Quick Sync DSM ecosystem, Direct Play, light legacy transcoding Older Gemini Lake Refresh; below Plex’s current Jasper Lake HEVC-output recommendation 
 The Most Important Rule: Buy the Video Engine, Not the CPU Benchmark
 Video transcoding is different from general CPU work.
 A powerful CPU can transcode in software, but modern Intel processors contain dedicated fixed-function video hardware through Intel Quick Sync Video . Plex and Jellyfin can use that hardware to decode and encode video while leaving most CPU resources available for the rest of the NAS .
 That is why an Intel N5095 NAS can be a better Plex purchase than a more powerful AMD Ryzen NAS that has no supported integrated media engine.
 Why Hardware Transcoding Matters
 Transcoding happens when the client cannot play the original file directly or when the requested stream must be changed.
 Remote bandwidth is lower than the source bitrate.
 The client does not support the source codec.
 The client requests a lower resolution.
 The audio format is incompatible.
 Subtitles must be burned into the picture.
 HDR video must be converted to SDR.
 Plex notes that transcoding is CPU-intensive and that hardware acceleration can make high-quality HEVC/4K conversion smoother while reducing the load and power consumption of the main CPU.
 Direct Play Is Still Better Than Transcoding
 The best transcode is the one you do not need.
 If your TV, streaming box, phone or browser can play the original container, codec, audio and subtitle combination, Plex or Jellyfin can use Direct Play .
 Direct Play requires very little server compute.
 A large 4K remux can still require substantial network bandwidth, but the NAS CPU is mostly reading the file and sending it to the client.
 If nearly everything in your home Direct Plays, spend money on:
 More drive bays.
 Larger HDDs.
 Better backup.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE where useful.
 Better client devices.
 rather than buying an expensive NAS only for a more powerful transcoder.
 Plex Hardware Acceleration Requires Plex Pass
 Plex currently requires an active Plex Pass subscription for normal hardware-accelerated streaming.
 When enabled, Plex can use supported Intel Quick Sync hardware for video decoding and encoding.
 In Plex:
 Settings
→ Server
→ Transcoder
→ Show Advanced
→ Use hardware acceleration when available 
 During playback, the Plex Dashboard should show (hw) beside the transcoded video path when hardware acceleration is actually working.
 Jellyfin Hardware Acceleration Does Not Need a Paid Licence
 Jellyfin supports several hardware-acceleration methods, including:
 Intel Quick Sync Video (QSV).
 Intel/AMD VA-API on Linux.
 NVIDIA NVENC/NVDEC.
 AMD AMF on Windows.
 For Intel NAS hardware, QSV or VA-API are the important choices.
 Jellyfin can accelerate multiple stages of the pipeline, including decoding, deinterlacing, scaling, HDR tone mapping and encoding when the hardware/software combination supports them.
 Best Overall: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus uses Intel’s 12th-generation Pentium Gold 8505.
 5 CPU cores / 6 threads.
 Up to 4.4GHz.
 Intel UHD Graphics.
 48 graphics execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 One multi-format codec engine.
 8GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 64GB RAM.
 1 × 10GbE + 1 × 2.5GbE.
 4 SATA bays + 2 M.2 slots.
 The 8505 is far newer than the J4125 and N5095 class and has substantially more general CPU headroom than either.
 That matters when Plex/Jellyfin shares the NAS with:
 Docker applications.
 Immich.
 Databases.
 Home Assistant services.
 Download automation.
 Media indexing.
 The built-in 10GbE port is unnecessary for one ordinary media stream, but useful when the same NAS also serves workstation backups, large file transfers or several clients.
 UGREEN’s main trade-off is software maturity. UGOS Pro has developed quickly, but QNAP and Synology have longer-established native NAS ecosystems.
 We cover the exact current UGREEN Plex/Jellyfin deployment and acceleration checks separately in Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding on UGREEN NASync .
 Best Modern Value Alternative: TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 The F4-425 Plus uses Intel’s newer N150 processor.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Up to 3.6GHz.
 6W processor base power.
 Intel Graphics with 24 execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 16GB DDR5 included.
 Up to 32GB RAM.
 2 × 5GbE.
 3 × M.2 PCIe 3.0 x1 slots.
 TerraMaster explicitly lists hardware transcoding for H.264, H.265, MPEG-4 and VC-1 on the F4-425 Plus, with the current product page advertising an 8K@60fps transcoding engine.
 The N150 is also newer than Plex’s “Jasper Lake or better” requirement for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS.
 This combination makes the F4-425 Plus particularly attractive when you want:
 A modern Intel media engine.
 Plenty of RAM out of the box.
 Fast networking.
 Four HDD bays.
 Docker/Jellyfin/Plex capability.
 Its general CPU is less capable than the UGREEN 8505, but a transcoding-first NAS often benefits more from the media engine than from extra CPU cores.
 Best Mature QNAP Option: TS-464
 The QNAP TS-464 uses Intel’s Celeron N5095.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 Up to 2.9GHz.
 Intel UHD Graphics.
 16 graphics execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 8GB DDR4 on the current 8G model.
 Up to 16GB officially supported RAM.
 2 × 2.5GbE.
 2 × M.2 PCIe Gen3 x1.
 PCIe Gen3 x2 expansion slot.
 The key detail is the CPU generation: N5095 is Jasper Lake .
 Plex currently says NAS users need Jasper Lake or better to reliably transcode to HEVC output. That keeps the TS-464 relevant even though its CPU is now old compared with an 8505 or N150.
 QNAP also explicitly lists hardware-accelerated transcoding as supported on the TS-464.
 Its strongest reasons to buy are:
 Mature QTS software.
 Container Station.
 Virtualization Station.
 Established Plex deployment history.
 PCIe expansion.
 HDMI 2.1 output.
 The main limitation is the 16GB official RAM ceiling. That matters more for a large home-lab stack than for Plex itself.
 Need Six Bays? QNAP TS-664 Uses the Same Media Platform
 The TS-664 uses the same N5095 CPU, graphics and 16GB memory ceiling as the TS-464.
 It therefore does not provide more transcoding compute.
 What it gives you is two additional SATA bays, which can be much more useful for a large movie/TV library.
 Choose TS-664 instead of TS-464 when the problem is media capacity , not transcoding speed.
 Best DSM Option: Synology DS425+—with a Major Caveat
 The DS425+ uses Intel’s Celeron J4125.
 4 cores / 4 threads.
 2.0GHz base / 2.7GHz burst.
 Intel UHD Graphics 600.
 12 execution units.
 Intel Quick Sync Video.
 2GB DDR4 included.
 Up to 6GB total RAM.
 1 × 2.5GbE + 1 × 1GbE.
 The DS425+ therefore does have an Intel hardware video engine.
 The problem is generation. Intel identifies J4125 as Gemini Lake Refresh , while Plex currently recommends Jasper Lake or better for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS.
 That makes the DS425+ reasonable for:
 Direct Play.
 Older H.264-heavy libraries.
 Occasional compatible hardware transcoding.
 Buyers who prioritise DSM over media-server performance.
 It is not our first choice for a new NAS bought specifically around modern HEVC transcoding.
 Why We Would Not Choose the Synology DS925+ for Transcoding
 The DS925+ is a stronger storage/server platform than the DS425+ in several areas: ECC RAM, 32GB memory support, eight CPU threads and expansion to nine bays.
 But its Ryzen V1500B does not provide an Intel Quick Sync media engine.
 For backups, Docker and storage growth, DS925+ can be the better NAS. For Plex/Jellyfin hardware transcoding, the older Intel DS425+ has the more useful architecture.
 A Fast AMD NAS Is Not Automatically a Fast Transcoding NAS
 This lesson extends beyond Synology.
 High-performance AMD systems such as the ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen3 can have much stronger CPU, ECC RAM and networking than an N5095 NAS.
 But if the processor does not expose a supported video encode/decode engine, Plex may need to use CPU software transcoding.
 Jellyfin supports AMD hardware acceleration when a suitable AMD GPU/APU is present, but not every Ryzen Embedded CPU includes the required graphics engine.
 HEVC Output Changed the CPU Generation Requirement
 Plex’s current hardware-accelerated streaming documentation includes an important NAS-specific line: Jasper Lake or better is required to reliably transcode to HEVC output .
 This matters because older NAS buying guides often treat any Quick Sync processor as equivalent.
 They are not.
 CPU Generation Current Plex HEVC-output position 
 J4125 Gemini Lake Refresh Older than current Jasper Lake recommendation 
 N5095 Jasper Lake Meets stated minimum generation 
 N150 Twin Lake Newer than stated minimum 
 Intel 8505 Alder Lake Newer than stated minimum 
 HEVC Encoding in Plex Is Still Experimental
 As of the current Plex transcoder documentation, HEVC video encoding is still marked experimental .
 Plex warns that HEVC encoding uses more resources and will generally support fewer concurrent streams than H.264.
 Do not buy a NAS based on an assumption such as “this will always transcode six 4K streams to HEVC”. Plex software, drivers, source files, HDR processing and subtitles can all change the result.
 HDR Tone Mapping Is a Separate Requirement
 Converting HDR video to SDR can add substantial processing work.
 Plex hardware tone mapping requires supported server software and compatible hardware. Plex currently notes an Intel Kaby Lake-or-newer requirement for relevant hardware-accelerated tone-mapping paths.
 Jellyfin supports hardware-accelerated HDR10/HLG tone mapping and supports Intel VPP tone mapping through QSV/VA-API on Linux.
 If your library is mostly 4K HDR remuxes and remote clients frequently need SDR, test this exact path—not simply “4K transcoding”.
 Subtitles Can Break an Otherwise Easy Transcode
 Subtitle format matters.
 Text subtitles such as SRT are often easier for clients to render directly. Image-based subtitles such as PGS may force subtitle burn-in depending on the client and playback path.
 Burn-in can move parts of the pipeline back to CPU processing and dramatically change performance.
 This is why “How many 4K streams?” is usually the wrong benchmark question.
 Docker Hardware Transcoding Works—but the Device Must Be Passed Through
 Plex explicitly supports hardware acceleration inside Docker when the host exposes a supported Intel Quick Sync device to the container.
 On a Linux-based Intel NAS, this normally means exposing the relevant /dev/dri device into the container and ensuring the container has the correct permissions.
 Jellyfin similarly requires access to the host’s GPU device and the appropriate QSV/VA-API configuration.
 If the container cannot see the iGPU, buying a Quick Sync CPU provides no hardware-transcoding benefit.
 Do Not Put Plex in a VM Expecting Quick Sync Automatically
 Plex’s current documentation says hardware-accelerated streaming is not supported inside ordinary virtual machines because the required low-level video hardware is not normally exposed to the guest.
 Advanced hypervisors can support PCIe/iGPU passthrough in other architectures, but that is a separate design problem.
 For an appliance NAS, Docker/native Plex is usually the cleaner hardware-transcoding path.
 RAM Matters Less for Transcoding Than People Think
 Plex itself does not need 64GB RAM to transcode video.
 Large memory capacity matters when the NAS also hosts:
 Immich.
 Nextcloud.
 Several databases.
 VMs.
 Large Docker stacks.
 RAM-based transcode temporary storage.
 For a pure Plex/Jellyfin box, modern Intel media hardware matters more than a huge RAM ceiling.
 SSD Cache Will Not Make Video Transcoding Faster by Magic
 A modern HDD can read one large movie file far faster than required for normal playback.
 SSD/NVMe is more useful for:
 Plex/Jellyfin metadata.
 Thumbnail databases.
 Transcode temporary files.
 Docker application data.
 Large multi-user metadata workloads.
 Store the bulk movie library on HDD unless silence, size or a specific high-performance workload justifies flash.
 1GbE Is Enough for Many Media Servers
 One Gigabit Ethernet connection can deliver roughly 100MB/s-plus of real application throughput under good conditions.
 That is far more than one ordinary compressed 4K stream needs.
 2.5GbE or 10GbE becomes valuable when the NAS also handles:
 Large workstation transfers.
 Multiple simultaneous users.
 Backups while media is streaming.
 Video editing.
 Several high-bitrate streams plus other NAS workloads.
 Do not buy a 10GbE NAS solely because you plan to watch one movie at a time.
 When a Mini PC Plus NAS Is Better
 If you need very strong transcoding but also want a large, long-lived storage array, separate compute and storage can be the better architecture.

 This lets you upgrade the media-server CPU without replacing the NAS enclosure and drive array.
 Our dedicated troubleshooting/buying article covers this decision: Plex Server vs NAS Storage: Which Component Should You Upgrade First? .
 Practical Buying Matrix

 Best NAS for Plex and Jellyfin Hardware Transcoding: The Bottom Line
 For a new purchase focused on transcoding, choose a modern Intel Quick Sync NAS. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is our strongest all-round hardware choice because its 8505 combines a modern media engine with much more general compute and RAM headroom than older NAS processors.
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus is a compelling media-first alternative with the newer N150, 16GB RAM and explicit hardware-transcoding support.
 The QNAP TS-464 remains highly relevant because N5095 is Jasper Lake, which matches Plex’s current minimum generation guidance for reliable HEVC-output transcoding on NAS, and QNAP’s software ecosystem is mature.
 The Synology DS425+ is the compromise choice. It provides DSM and Quick Sync, but its Gemini Lake Refresh J4125 is older than Plex’s current HEVC-output recommendation. Buy it for DSM and Direct Play, not because it is the strongest new transcoding platform.
 Above all, check whether you actually need transcoding. If your clients Direct Play your library, the best Plex NAS may simply be the NAS with the right number of drive bays, reliable backups and the software ecosystem you prefer.

If every file you own direct-plays without conversion, the Synology DS923+ will happily serve more simultaneous 4K streams than either of them, because it never has to touch its CPU. The one fact to settle before you compare anything else: hardware transcoding needs an Intel integrated GPU and a paid Plex Pass — an AMD-based NAS cannot do it at all, no matter how fast its processor is.

 Best overall: TerraMaster F4-424 Pro
 The F4-424 Pro is the pick when transcoding is the job. Per TerraMaster’s spec sheet, its Core i3-N305 pairs a 32-execution-unit Intel UHD iGPU with 8 GB of DDR5 that expands to 32 GB — more headroom than the Celeron-class boxes it undercuts on price. In practice that translates to roughly four to five simultaneous 4K-to-1080p transcodes, and about half that if Plex is tone-mapping HDR to SDR at the same time.
 Who it suits: households with a mix of clients — an Apple TV 4K, a couple of phones, a browser tab — where somebody is always forcing a conversion. Main trade-off: TerraMaster’s TOS software is less polished than Synology’s DSM or QNAP’s QTS, and the third-party app catalog is thinner. You are buying silicon, not software.
 Best value four-bay: QNAP TS-464
 The TS-464 uses a Celeron N5095 with a 16-EU iGPU, 8 GB of DDR4 (16 GB max), dual 2.5GbE ports and two M.2 NVMe slots for cache or a separate metadata volume. It handles two to three 4K transcodes comfortably and will direct-play everything you throw at it. QTS is a mature platform with a proper container station, which matters if you want to run Plex alongside the *arr stack.
 Who it suits: the buyer who wants a proven four-bay chassis and doesn’t want to learn a new operating system. Main trade-off: roughly half the transcoding throughput of the N305 for only about $50–$100 less, and QNAP’s firmware cadence means occasional update babysitting.
 Best small starter box: Synology DS224+
 The DS224+ is the cheapest route into genuine Quick Sync transcoding. Its Celeron J4125 and 12-EU iGPU will push one, occasionally two, 4K-to-1080p conversions, and DSM remains the easiest NAS operating system to live with. The catch is the 2 GB of soldered RAM — plan on adding a stick to reach the 6 GB ceiling, because Plex’s metadata and thumbnail database is memory-hungry.
 Who it suits: a first NAS for one or two viewers, or a secondary box for a bedroom. Main trade-off: two bays means RAID 1 gives you only one drive’s worth of usable capacity, and there is no upgrade path except replacing the whole unit.
 Best for large 4K libraries: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 The DXP4800 Plus is the only pick here with 10GbE built in, and its Pentium Gold 8505 carries a 48-EU iGPU — the strongest transcode engine in this group, good for five to six simultaneous 4K-to-1080p conversions. DDR5 expands to 64 GB, which is overkill for Plex but welcome if you also run virtual machines. The 10GbE port matters more than it sounds: a 4K remux peaks around 80–100 Mbps, so a 1GbE link saturates at roughly nine direct streams before overhead, while 10GbE removes the network as a bottleneck entirely.
 Who it suits: anyone with a 20 TB-plus remux collection and a wired 10GbE switch or a direct-attach workstation. Main trade-off: UGOS is the youngest operating system in this roundup, and the ecosystem is still catching up on polish.
 Best for direct-play purists: Synology DS923+
 Per Synology’s spec sheet, the DS923+’s AMD Ryzen R1600 has no integrated graphics — which means no Quick Sync, which means every conversion falls to two cores of CPU. Software-transcoding 4K HEVC on that chip is not realistic; it will stutter. But if your clients all direct-play, the DS923+ is arguably the best pure file server here: ECC memory support, a PCIe slot for a 10GbE card, and DSM’s mature storage management.
 Who it suits: a library encoded in formats your players already understand, or a household that keeps a separate mini-PC as the Plex server and uses the NAS purely for storage. Main trade-off: buy it expecting to transcode and you will be disappointed.
 How to choose: the numbers that actually matter
 1. Confirm you need transcoding at all
 Direct play uses no CPU — the NAS just streams bytes. Transcoding happens when the client can’t handle the file’s codec, container, resolution or subtitle format, or when remote viewers are capped by upload bandwidth. Check your library and your players first; if everything direct-plays, you can spend the transcoding budget on drive bays instead.
 2. Budget for Plex Pass, because hardware transcoding is locked behind it
 Plex’s documentation is explicit: GPU-accelerated transcoding is a Plex Pass feature. Without it, the iGPU sits idle and Plex falls back to software encoding. A lifetime pass costs roughly the same as one extra drive, and it is the single highest-value purchase in this entire build.
 3. Count bays by capacity, not by ambition
 A 4-bay chassis in RAID 5 or Synology’s SHR gives you three drives of usable space plus one for parity. A 2-bay in RAID 1 gives you one. If your library is 15 TB and growing, two bays means buying two 20 TB drives to store 20 TB — four bays means four 8 TB drives to store 24 TB, usually for less money.
 4. Match the network port to your peak bitrate
 Add up the peak bitrate of your busiest simultaneous streams and leave 30% headroom. Three 4K remuxes at 90 Mbps is 270 Mbps, which 1GbE handles fine. Ten of them is 900 Mbps, which it does not — that is when 2.5GbE or 10GbE stops being a luxury.
 Worked example: sizing a 4-bay NAS for a 400-film 4K library
 Assume 400 UHD remuxes at an average of 60 GB each. That is 24,000 GB, or about 24 TB of media. Add Plex metadata: artwork and database files run a few gigabytes, but generated video thumbnails can consume 100 GB or more on a large library, so budget 25 TB total.
 Four 12 TB NAS drives in RAID 5 give 36 TB raw usable, minus roughly 10% for filesystem overhead, landing near 32 TB. That leaves about 7 TB of growth room. At typical 2026 pricing of $15–$20 per terabyte for NAS-rated CMR drives, the storage costs $720–$960, on top of a $450–$650 chassis — call it $1,200–$1,600 all in, or roughly $3–$4 per film stored.
 Now the transcoding side: a 16-EU Celeron iGPU handles two to three 4K-to-1080p conversions; a 32-EU i3-N305 handles four to five; a 48-EU Pentium Gold handles five to six. Enable HDR tone mapping and cut every one of those numbers roughly in half, because tone mapping is a second GPU pass on the same silicon.

 Ownership realities: what wears out and what trips people up
 Drives fail first. NAS-rated CMR disks are typically rated around one million hours MTBF, which in a four-drive array usually means one failure somewhere in years three to five. Buy drives from different batches and keep a cold spare on the shelf.
 Avoid SMR drives. Shingled magnetic recording drives stall badly during RAID rebuilds. Check the spec sheet for “CMR” before you buy — this is the most common costly mistake in budget NAS builds.
 SSD cache is not a transcoding upgrade. It accelerates metadata and random I/O, not GPU work. If you have two M.2 slots, one cache drive plus one dedicated volume for Plex metadata is a better split than two mirrored cache drives.
 RAID is not a backup. It survives a dead disk; it does not survive an accidental delete, ransomware, or a power surge. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two media types, one off-site.
 Heat and dust are the slow killers. Keep ambient temperature under 30°C, clean the intake filters every three to six months, and expect fans to be the first non-drive component to need replacing.
 Wire it. Wi-Fi adds jitter and typically halves usable throughput; a NAS on wireless will stutter on high-bitrate 4K even when the CPU is idle.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I run Plex on a NAS without an Intel CPU?
 Yes, but only with software transcoding. AMD-based units like the Synology DS923+ handle direct play perfectly well and can serve several 4K streams at once, since streaming without conversion costs almost no CPU. The moment a client forces a 4K HEVC conversion, however, a low-power AMD chip will not keep up and playback will buffer.
 Do I really need a Plex Pass for hardware transcoding?
 Yes. Plex’s documentation lists GPU-accelerated transcoding as a Plex Pass feature, so without a subscription the integrated GPU stays idle and everything falls back to CPU encoding. This is why two NAS units with identical processors can perform completely differently — the difference is the license, not the hardware.
 How many simultaneous 4K streams can a NAS handle?
 Direct play is limited by disk and network, not CPU: on 1GbE expect roughly five to nine concurrent 4K remux streams before the link saturates. Hardware transcoding is limited by the iGPU: two to three streams on a 16-EU Celeron, four to five on a 32-EU Core i3-N305, and five to six on a 48-EU Pentium Gold. Enabling HDR tone mapping roughly halves each figure.
 Is RAID enough to protect my media library?
 No. RAID protects against a single drive failure by keeping the array running; it does nothing about deletion, corruption, theft or fire, because every change is mirrored instantly to the parity drive. Treat RAID as uptime insurance and keep a separate backup — for a large remux library, an external drive rotation or a second NAS at another address is the practical approach.
 How much RAM does a Plex NAS actually need?
 Plex itself is light, but the metadata database and thumbnail generation are not. Four gigabytes is a reasonable floor for a library of a few hundred titles; eight gigabytes is comfortable; more than sixteen only pays off if you also run virtual machines or containers. On the Synology DS224+, the 2 GB stock configuration is genuinely tight — upgrading to 6 GB is the first thing to do.
 Should I buy a 2-bay or a 4-bay NAS for Plex?
 Buy four bays unless space or budget is genuinely tight. A 2-bay array in RAID 1 wastes half your raw capacity on mirroring, so storing 20 TB requires two 20 TB drives — often more expensive than four 8 TB drives in RAID 5, which would give you 24 TB usable. Four bays also let you expand one drive at a time instead of replacing the whole unit.

 Choosing a 6-bay NAS for a large 4K media library is about much more than finding six empty drive bays. I compared the processors, memory, network ports, expansion options, and real-world feedback for six current models, focusing on the point where a quiet home media server stops merely storing movies and starts delivering them smoothly to several screens at once.
 My top recommendation is the UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Plus because its Intel Core i3 processor, 10GbE port, DDR5 memory, and high drive-capacity ceiling make it the strongest all-round package for 4K direct play and demanding software transcoding. The other picks each serve a narrower need, from QNAP’s 10GbE value model to an ASUSTOR system built with video creators in mind.
 This roundup reflects the specifications, customer feedback, and limitations available for each diskless enclosure. I have not added drive costs to the decision, because two homes buying the same NAS can need completely different disks, and storage media should follow library size, redundancy needs, and acceptable noise.

 A 10GbE port plus a 2.5GbE port makes local transfers much less dependent on a mechanical-disk ceiling. That matters when you are adding 4K remuxes, repairing a RAID array, or moving a season of high-bitrate HDR files to the NAS before anyone starts watching.
 UGREEN includes 8GB of DDR5 and a built-in 128GB SSD, while the enclosure leaves two M.2 NVMe positions available for cache or additional fast storage. I would still verify the current app and container compatibility before planning a production workflow around those slots.
 How does the Intel i3 handle 4K transcoding?
 The i3-1215U is the most convincing CPU in this roundup for simultaneous media work. It is far better suited than entry-level Celeron silicon to the sustained H.264 or HEVC work created when several clients request incompatible 4K streams.
 Direct play remains the best-looking and least CPU-intensive route because the television, streaming box, or player receives the file without re-encoding it. Hardware media acceleration can help when a client cannot decode HDR10, Dolby Vision, a high bitrate, or an unsupported audio track, but the actual codec path and Plex support need to be checked in the installed app.
 Does 10GbE make a real difference for 4K movies?
 For a single direct-play stream, a well-tuned 1GbE link can often carry a high-bitrate 4K file, but 10GbE removes more of the uncertainty around network overhead and concurrent users. It is most valuable when the NAS is also serving files, running backups, and streaming to several rooms at the same time.
 The 2.5GbE port gives you a practical second lane for link aggregation, a separate network, or a client that does not have 10GbE. A 10GbE switch, compatible client adapter, and cabling are additional pieces of the installation, so I would treat 10GbE as a performance feature rather than a promise of a specific movie bitrate.
 Is six bays enough for a growing 4K library?
 UGREEN specifies a maximum of 208TB across the six SATA bays, which gives this chassis unusually large expansion headroom. Actual usable capacity depends on drive size and RAID choice, and mixed replacement sizes can make future rebuilds less straightforward.
 For a first setup, I would choose equal-capacity drives and use a redundant array if the library is important. A single large archive is still worth keeping a separate backup, since RAID improves availability but does not protect every copy of a file from deletion, malware, or a NAS failure.

 Why are two PCIe slots useful in a media server?
 They let you separate network upgrades from other add-in functions. Depending on the supported card and QTS configuration, that can mean a faster NIC, an SSD cache card, or a supported GPU for video processing.
 Do not buy a graphics card based on a generic “GPU support” claim. Check the NAS firmware compatibility list, card power limits, cooler clearance, and the codec workload you expect to run; unsupported software paths can turn a powerful card into an expensive paperweight.
 Can 2.5GbE keep up with 4K remuxes?
 It is a sensible baseline for several 4K streams when the source is stored on local disks and the network is clean. It does not match the headroom of a dedicated 10GbE connection, and it cannot remove the CPU cost of real-time transcoding.
 For clients that direct play, use a wired 2.5GbE path where possible and keep Wi-Fi 6 or a faster wireless backbone for portable devices. For clients that force transcoding, prioritize a stronger processor or supported hardware acceleration over buying a faster switch by itself.
 Who benefits most from Qtier and M.2 caching?
 Small files, application data, and frequently accessed media folders benefit more from SSD acceleration than a large sequential movie file already streaming from a healthy array. Qtier can move hot data between tiers, while M.2 storage can serve as a cache or a separate fast volume.
 If your library is mostly archival 4K video, invest in the drive array, PSU, cooling, and network first. Use SSD acceleration for metadata, downloads, photo libraries, and active project folders where random performance matters.

A 4K file that is merely being copied or streamed unchanged asks much less of the CPU than a file that must be decoded and encoded in real time.
 Before committing, I would test representative HDR10 and Dolby Vision files, turn off unnecessary transcoding where direct play works, and avoid assuming that “4K-ready” on a specification sheet means every 4K format will transcode equally well.

 They can hold NVMe SSDs for cache or supported fast-storage tasks. For a media archive, that can improve active folders, metadata services, and application performance without replacing the six SATA drives.

 How to Choose the Best 6-Bay NAS for Your 4K Media Library
 The right choice depends on whether your 4K files will direct play, transcode, and how many people may watch at the same time. Use these decisions in order rather than choosing a NAS by drive count alone.
 Start with direct play versus transcoding
 Direct play means the player receives the original video stream. It preserves quality, uses less NAS CPU, and is usually the best result when the client supports the video codec, HDR format, bitrate, and audio track.
 Transcoding means the NAS decodes and re-encodes the file, often because a client cannot play the original format. Several simultaneous transcodes demand a stronger Intel Core i3 or comparable processor, while a modest Celeron or ARM system is better reserved for direct play and light workloads.
 HDR10 and Dolby Vision deserve extra attention. A NAS can direct play HDR10 to a compatible display, but Dolby Vision profiles and device support can vary, and a direct-play path may still need an audio or subtitle change.
 Plan RAID around availability, not only capacity
 RAID 5 uses parity across the drives and gives usable space equal to roughly the capacity of all but one drive, while RAID 6 reserves two-drive parity for extra protection. A 6-bay NAS makes either layout practical, but the array choice should follow how much rebuild risk you can tolerate.
 For a replaceable media collection, a less redundant layout may make more space available. For family photos, recordings, or a library you cannot easily replace, favor redundancy and keep a separate backup because RAID is not a substitute for an independent copy.
 Install identical drives where possible, record the model and serial numbers, and schedule a maintenance window for scrubbing. Six large drives take time to rebuild, and leaving little free space can make the process harder.
 Count storage before choosing drive sizes
 A 4K movie can range from roughly 10GB to more than 100GB depending on length, compression, frame rate, and whether it is a streaming copy or a full remux. A library of 100 movies therefore needs far more planning than a folder of a few downloaded films.
 Use a simple capacity model: estimate the average gigabytes per title, multiply by the number of titles, then add headroom for metadata, future 4K releases, and temporary downloads. A separate backup can require another full copy, so the final storage number may be larger than the playable library itself.
 Do not fill every bay immediately if the library will grow. Equal-capacity drives simplify expansion, while mixed sizes can force you to replace several disks or accept an unexpectedly small usable pool.
 Match networking to the number of streams
 1GbE is a useful starting point for a single direct-playing client, but it is easy to reach its practical ceiling when several devices stream, download, and back up at once. 2.5GbE is a sensible middle ground, while 10GbE is most valuable for fast file transfers and a network serving many active users.
 Use wired Ethernet for televisions, NVIDIA SHIELD-style players, desktop clients, and other stationary 4K devices where possible. Wi-Fi can work well with a strong wireless backbone, but wireless contention and weak signal can make an otherwise capable NAS look like it is buffering.
 A fast network cannot fix a CPU bottleneck. If clients force transcoding, prioritize processor and hardware-media support first, then upgrade the switch and cabling.
 Keep noise, power, and heat under control
 A 6-bay NAS with six hard drives may run all day and all night. The supplied forum insights repeatedly identify 24/7 power use and living-room noise as common pain points, so I would compare idle fan behavior, drive vibration, and the location of the chassis before installation.
 Use NAS-rated hard drives, provide open airflow around the enclosure, and avoid putting a six-bay unit inside a closed TV cabinet. A small UPS can protect the array from abrupt outages, though it should be sized for the NAS and connected equipment rather than chosen by wattage alone.
 Power efficiency also depends on the workload. A Celeron or ARM NAS can be quiet and efficient for direct play, while an i3 system may use more power but finish demanding work sooner and handle more concurrent streams.
 Choose software and expansion as a package
 QTS, ASUSTOR’s ADM-based platform, and UGREEN’s management software each have their own app catalog and setup style. Community feedback praises QNAP’s feature set and UGREEN’s performance value, while forum discussions also warn that software familiarity and documentation matter when a media server becomes part of daily life.
 For Plex, check the current app’s hardware-acceleration support before buying. Plex Pass requirements can change, and the same CPU can behave differently with H.264, HEVC, VP9, audio passthrough, HDR10, and Dolby Vision.
 I would also check RAM limits, M.2 compatibility, drive format support, expansion-slot clearance, and warranty terms. A NAS that looks capable on paper can become a poor value if its key upgrade path is closed or its support process is difficult.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Which NAS is best for streaming 4K content?
 The UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Plus is our best overall pick for 4K media because it combines a 12th-generation Intel Core i3 processor with 10GbE networking, 8GB of DDR5, six SATA bays, and two M.2 NVMe slots. Choose it when several users, container workloads, or occasional transcoding are likely.
 Which NAS is best for streaming 4K content on Plex?
 For Plex, choose based on the client path: the UGREEN DXP6800 Plus offers the strongest CPU and expansion headroom in this group, while the QNAP TS-632X-4G-US is a value-oriented option for direct play and fast 10GbE transfers. The QNAP TS-673A-8G is attractive when PCIe or GPU expansion matters.
 Can a NAS run Plex Media Server?
 Yes. A NAS can run Plex Media Server when its operating system supports the Plex package or container, and it can stream files over Ethernet or Wi-Fi. Hardware acceleration and transcoding quality depend on the NAS processor, the Plex app version, the codec, and the playback client.
 What is the best NAS for Plex Media Server in 2026?
 For a large 4K library in 2026, the UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Plus is the strongest all-round choice here. The QNAP TS-673A-8G is better for users who value PCIe and GPU expansion, and the TS-632X-4G-US is the value pick when 10GbE matters more than heavy transcoding.
 How many GB should a 4K movie be?
 There is no single size. A 4K movie may be around 10GB or exceed 100GB, depending on its runtime, compression, bitrate, frame rate, and whether it is a streaming encode or a full remux; estimate from your own library and leave room for metadata, future releases, and backups.
 Final Verdict: Which 6-Bay NAS Should You Buy?
 The best 6-bay NAS for most large 4K media libraries is the UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Plus. It gives you a stronger Intel i3 processor, a 10GbE connection, 8GB of DDR5, six bays, and a much more comfortable path through demanding Plex and container workloads.
 Choose the QNAP TS-632X-4G-US when 10GbE value, quiet operation, and expandable memory matter most. Choose the TS-673A-8G when PCIe expansion or supported GPU acceleration is part of your plan, and choose the ASUSTOR AS6706T v2 for a creator-focused hybrid of media, Docker, and NVMe storage.
 My practical buying test is simple: make a 20-movie test library, include your most demanding HDR and audio combinations, and confirm the actual clients direct play them. That small test tells you more about buffering and compatibility than a processor name alone, and it makes the final decision much easier.
